title: WTF do people use Open Models for??

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on Featherless.ai as a platform providing API access to 3,700+ open models, analyzing usage patterns and offering developer infrastructure for building AI systems. Featherless.ai is a developer platform for model hosting and API access, while usage data spans general-purpose applications across multiple verticals. Discussion focuses on production deployment patterns, model staying power, and reliability engineering for live AI systems. Requires familiarity with open model ecosystem, API platforms, and production AI concepts but not deep technical implementation. Conference presentation with usage data charts and platform demonstrations. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript with supporting excerpts.

summary: Eugene Cheah of Featherless.ai shares platform data revealing what people actually use open models for. Over 50,000 models are uploaded to Hugging Face monthly. DeepSeek R1 emerged as a breakthrough open model matching GPT-4 with 4 million downloads and 2.74 exabytes transferred. Featherless offers flat $25/month unlimited access to 3,700+ open models, enabling usage analysis without token-based pricing distortions. Users choose models by vibes and fame rather than benchmarks. Model staying power is a key surprise: 8-month-old Mistral Nemo remains dominant in production due to enterprise consistency needs, Apache 2.0 licensing, and cost advantages. Usage segments by volume: creativity/companionship (30-40%), coding (20-30%), RAG/ChatGPT clones (~20%), agents/work (10-20%), and ComfyUI workflows (~5%). Coding shifted from auto-completion to agentic 'vibe coding,' where developers generate ~1000x more tokens than companionship users. Claude Sonnet dominates agentic coding at a 10:1 ratio. Open source projects Cline and Continue combined rival Cursor with open models. For production AI agents, Eugene strongly advises starting with 80-90% automation plus human escape hatches, iterating toward 99.998% reliability. Teams pursuing 100% automation without escape hatches risk catastrophic failures. The talk concludes with Quirky, a 72B parameter linear Transformer-attention hybrid costing only $100K to build versus DeepSeek's $10M, running at less than half the compute cost of standard Transformers. Eugene closes by questioning whether frontier benchmark capabilities like orbital re-entry calculations matter when most AI agents still can't be trusted with a single task without hallucination. He expresses excitement about linear Transformer models for persisting memories, customization, and improving reliability, and invites organizations to run Featherless or Quirky in private cloud or on-premise environments.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Open Model Scale and DeepSeek R1 Impact
sections.summary: Eugene introduces the scale of open model proliferation: 50,000+ models uploaded monthly to Hugging Face. DeepSeek R1 is highlighted as the breakthrough open model surpassing GPT-4 with 4 million downloads and 2.74 exabytes of data transfer.

sections.title: Featherless.ai Platform and Data Source
sections.summary: Eugene introduces Featherless.ai offering unlimited API access to 3,700+ open models at $25/month flat pricing, enabling unique insights into actual open model usage patterns across individual and commercial users.

sections.title: Individual User Model Preferences
sections.summary: Individual user data from February 2025 shows DeepSeek R1 dominant, followed by Llama, Mistral Nemo, and Qwen. Flat pricing means users choose by preference, vibes, and model fame rather than benchmarks or cost. Fine-tuning fragmentation reveals large models sliced into personality-specific variants.

sections.title: Model Staying Power in Production
sections.summary: Despite newer better models, the 8-month-old Mistral Nemo dominates commercial workloads due to Apache 2.0 licensing, enterprise consistency needs, cost advantages of small models, and tutorial stickiness. Llama 2 Guard persists as the default safeguard model. Enterprises avoid changing models once they achieve 99%+ accuracy.

sections.title: AI Usage Categories by Volume
sections.summary: Usage sorted by volume: creativity/companionship, code, commodity UI, writing/checking, and agents/work. Data sourced from direct customer usage and exchanged with OpenRouter.

sections.title: Creative Writing, Roleplay, and Companionship
sections.summary: This segment represents 30-40% of non-coding AI traffic with tens of millions of users. Apps like NovelCrafter serve writers while Wy Chat and S Haven serve companionship. Over 60% of companionship users are women, mirroring romance novel sales. Users value emotional availability and slow-burn interactions. Community fine-tunes create constantly changing personality models.

sections.title: Coding Co-pilot and Agents
sections.summary: Coding represents 20-30% of traffic, split between auto-completion tools like GitHub Copilot and chat-based editing available through IDE plugins.

sections.title: Vibe Coding and Agentic Coding Tools
sections.summary: Auto-completion for code is essentially solved with small 3B-12B models. The battleground has moved to agentic coding or 'vibe coding' where developers chat and prompt changes without touching code. A single vibe-coding developer generates ~1000x more tokens than a companionship user. Claude Sonnet dominates this use case at over 10:1 ratio. Open source projects Cline (agentic chat) and Continue (auto-completion) combine to rival Cursor with open models, including running on private local clusters offline.

sections.title: ComfyUI and Creative Agentic Workflows
sections.summary: ComfyUI and similar graph-style workflow tools represent ~5% of traffic. Originally used for diffusion image generation, these tools now serve non-developer power users like reporters, lawyers, musicians, and influencers chaining complex text generation workflows. Unlike coding agents, this segment shows slow gradual user growth over months rather than sudden spikes.

sections.title: RAG and ChatGPT Clones
sections.summary: RAG and ChatGPT clones represent ~20% of all requests. Every API provider has their own internal ChatGPT UI. TypingMind is highlighted as a standout application with a one-time fee model instead of subscription, usable locally against any API provider, with strong UI polish and a plugin system.

sections.title: AI for Agents and Work: Workflow Automation
sections.summary: AI for agents and work represents 10-20% of traffic, split into workflow automation (narrow agents) and fully automated agents. For workflow automation, the priority is production deployment with human escape hatches from day one. Pattern: AI drafts 80-90% of responses, humans review and send. Insurance and logistics companies automate email responses this way. Over time, reliable use cases get fully automated after seeing thousands of examples.

sections.title: Fully Automated Agents and Reliability Engineering
sections.summary: Fully 100% reliable autonomous agents do not exist in production; everyone who has tried has been burned. Eugene advises solving 80% with escape hatches, then iterating 80-90% of the remaining failures repeatedly to reach 99.998% reliability, following reliability engineering principles. He urges enterprises to upgrade from Llama 2 and calls on closed-source labs to provide version stability.

sections.title: Quirky: Post-Transformer Hybrid Model and Closing Remarks
sections.summary: Eugene introduces Quirky, a 72B parameter linear Transformer and attention Transformer hybrid costing only $100K to build versus DeepSeek's $10M, running at less than half the compute cost of standard Transformers. He closes by questioning the relevance of frontier benchmarks like orbital re-entry calculations when most AI agents still can't be trusted with a single task without hallucination. He expresses excitement about linear Transformer models for persisting memories, customization, and improving reliability, and invites organizations to run Featherless or Quirky in private cloud or on-premise environments.
